title: Cooking & Baking
strapline: Flour on the floor, science in the bowl, and something warm to share at the end — cooking is the whole curriculum with a wooden spoon.
intent: Children see irreversible change happen in front of them — dough rising, butter melting, egg turning solid, sugar dissolving — and start asking why.
Children follow a real sequence with a real consequence: miss a step and the cake tells you.
Children measure, count and compare for a genuine purpose — two eggs, three spoonfuls, is the jug full yet?
Children build the hand skills of the kitchen: pouring, spreading, stirring, kneading, cutting with a table knife.
Children meet food from many kitchens — the dishes, festivals and family recipes of everyone in the room — and taste more widely because they made it themselves.
Children learn kitchen hygiene and safety as habits: wash hands first, hot things are the adult's job, we taste at the end.
implementation: Use a picture recipe card with photographed steps so children can 'read' the sequence themselves and tell you what comes next.
Give every child real jobs, not watching turns — one cracks, one whisks, one spoons the cases; rotate across the recipe.
Narrate the science at the moment it happens: 'watch the butter — it's melting, it was solid, now it's runny'. Wonder aloud, don't lecture.
Count and measure out loud together, letting children fill, level and tip the spoonfuls even when it's slower.
Invite family recipes in — a parent cooking their dish with the children beats any recipe an adult found online.
Cook what you grow whenever the garden allows — herbs into bread, strawberries onto scones closes a loop children remember.
Revisit the sequence afterwards with the photos: 'what did we do first? then what?' — the retell embeds the learning.
key_questions: What do you think will happen when it goes in the oven?
What changed when we mixed it — where did the sugar go?
What did we do first? What came next?
How many spoonfuls do we need — shall we count them in?
Who cooks at your house — what do they make?

impact.text: Children pour, spread, stir and spoon mixture with growing control, managing jugs and spoons at their own pace.
Children use kitchen tools with intent — whisks, cutters, table knives for spreading and chopping soft foods.
Children notice and comment on change as they cook — melting, dissolving, rising, setting.
Children count spoonfuls and eggs into the bowl and judge full, half-full and 'too much' as they measure.
Children recount the recipe in order afterwards — first we washed hands, then we cracked the eggs — using the photo cards.
Children use new kitchen words in context — knead, dissolve, ingredients, sizzle.
Children talk about who cooks at home and what they make, noticing that families and their food differ — and that's interesting.
Children taste what they've made — including foods new to them — and can tell you about something they've cooked.

enhancements: Bread week: knead it, watch it rise (photograph the bowl every ten minutes), bake it, butter it warm.
A family recipe book built one cooking session at a time, with photos, and each family's dish in their own words.
Butter in a jar — cream plus shaking plus every child's turn equals butter, the fastest kitchen science there is.
A herb-and-smell tray from the garden: snip, crush, sniff and choose what goes in today's bread.
Festival baking through the year, led where possible by the families who celebrate — pancakes, mince pies, and the festivals of every family in the room.
Playdough made by the children from the real recipe — measuring and mixing where getting it wrong is cheap.
A 'we made this' plate at snack time so the whole room tastes what the cooking group produced.

playing_exploring: Flour, dough and mixture are irresistible sensory materials — with the bonus that these ones become food.
Children have a go at every job, including the awkward ones like cracking eggs.
active_learning: A recipe is a project with a finish line — children hold the goal (cake!) through every step.
Waiting for the oven, and finding it worth it, is delayed gratification made delicious.
creating_thinking: Children predict what heat and mixing will do, then watch their prediction meet reality.
They connect the sequence to the outcome — flat biscuits invite the question 'what did we forget?'
